title: Taiwan Passes Law to Pay Health Insurance for Most Seniors
summaryZh: 立法院三讀，65歲以上多數長者健保費將由中央全額補助。
summaryHi: ताइवान की संसद ने 65+ अधिकांश बुज़ुर्गों का स्वास्थ्य बीमा प्रीमियम सरकार से भरवाने का कानून पास किया।
summaryEs: Taiwán aprueba que el Gobierno pague el seguro de salud de la mayoría de los mayores de 65.
summaryJa: 台湾立法院、65歳以上の大半の高齢者の健康保険料を政府が全額負担する改正案を可決。
summaryKo: 대만 입법원, 65세 이상 대부분 노인의 건강보험료를 정부가 전액 부담하는 법안 통과.
summaryEn: Taiwan's legislature voted to have the government pay health insurance premiums for most people over 65.
paragraphs: Taiwan's opposition-controlled legislature on Friday passed an amendment requiring the central government to cover the National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums of most residents aged 65 and over, just six weeks before local elections.

The change to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, proposed by the Kuomintang and the Taiwan People's Party, was approved by 60 votes to 39. It applies to seniors whose income falls below the tax-filing threshold or is taxed at under 20 percent, which this year means net income of NT$1.38 million or less.

The TPP said the measure fulfils a 2024 campaign pledge by its founder, Ko Wen-je, who introduced similar subsidies while serving as Taipei mayor. Several local governments copied the idea, but financially stretched counties with large elderly populations were unable to follow.

Health Minister Shih Chung-liang criticised the amendment, arguing that it breaks the principle that contributions should reflect ability to pay. He warned it could create unfairness between generations, push up premiums for others and force the government to divert tax money from other welfare programmes.

Taiwan is now a super-aged society, with one in five people over 65, and that group accounts for more than 42 percent of NHI spending. The TPP estimates the subsidy will cost almost NT$39 billion a year.
Taiwan's lawmakers passed a new law on Friday. The law is about health insurance for older people.
In Taiwan, everyone pays a small amount of money every month for health care. This money is called a premium. Under the new law, the government will pay this money for many people aged 65 and over.
Not every older person can get this help. People with a very high income must still pay. But most older people will not pay anymore. The help is about NT$826 a month for each person.
Two opposition parties, the KMT and the TPP, wanted the law. The vote was 60 to 39. Local elections are in six weeks.

The health minister is not happy. He says the plan will cost a lot of money, about NT$39 billion every year. He is worried that the health system will have problems in the future. "An election is short, but people need the health system for a long time," he said.
Taiwan's legislature passed a change to the law on Friday that will make the government pay health insurance premiums for most people aged 65 and over. The vote was 60 to 39.

The change was proposed by the two main opposition parties, the Kuomintang (KMT) and the Taiwan People's Party (TPP). Seniors will qualify if their yearly income is low enough to pay tax at a rate below 20 percent. This year, that means a net income of NT$1.38 million or less.

The TPP said the law keeps a promise made in 2024 by its founder, Ko Wen-je. When he was mayor of Taipei, the city already paid premiums for older residents. Some other cities did the same, but poorer areas with many old people could not afford it.

The TPP thinks the plan will cost nearly NT$39 billion a year. Health Minister Shih Chung-liang is against it. He said the national health insurance system is based on people paying according to their ability, and this change could damage it.
Shih also warned that young people might pay more in the future. "An election is temporary," he said, "but people rely on the health system." Local elections will be held in six weeks.

Taiwan's opposition-controlled legislature on Friday passed an amendment requiring the central government to cover the National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums of most residents aged 65 and over, just six weeks before local elections.

The change to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, proposed by the Kuomintang and the Taiwan People's Party, was approved by 60 votes to 39. It applies to seniors whose income falls below the tax-filing threshold or is taxed at under 20 percent, which this year means net income of NT$1.38 million or less.

The TPP said the measure fulfils a 2024 campaign pledge by its founder, Ko Wen-je, who introduced similar subsidies while serving as Taipei mayor. Several local governments copied the idea, but financially stretched counties with large elderly populations were unable to follow.

Health Minister Shih Chung-liang criticised the amendment, arguing that it breaks the principle that contributions should reflect ability to pay. He warned it could create unfairness between generations, push up premiums for others and force the government to divert tax money from other welfare programmes.

Taiwan is now a super-aged society, with one in five people over 65, and that group accounts for more than 42 percent of NHI spending. The TPP estimates the subsidy will cost almost NT$39 billion a year.

With local elections only six weeks away, Taiwan's opposition parties have pushed through legislation that will see the state pick up the health insurance bills of the vast majority of the country's seniors.

The amendment to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, sponsored by the Kuomintang and the Taiwan People's Party, cleared the legislature 60 to 39 on Friday. Anyone aged 65 or older whose taxable income is below the filing threshold, or taxed at less than 20 percent, will have their National Health Insurance premiums paid in full by the central government.

For the TPP, the vote delivers on a 2024 presidential campaign promise by its founding chairman, Ko Wen-je, who pioneered such subsidies as mayor of Taipei. Other municipalities followed suit, though cash-strapped counties with ageing populations could not afford to.

The government reacted with alarm. Health Minister Shih Chung-liang said the measure undermines the system's core principle that people contribute according to their means, and cautioned that the true fiscal cost could exceed the TPP's estimate of nearly NT$39 billion a year. "An election is temporary," he remarked, "but the NHI system is something people rely on."
The dispute reflects deeper demographic pressure: residents over 65 now make up a fifth of the population and consume more than 42 percent of NHI spending.

Taiwan's legislature has approved a contentious amendment that obliges the central government to fund the National Health Insurance premiums of most citizens aged 65 and above, a move critics have characterised as an expensive pre-election gesture.

Sponsored by the opposition Kuomintang and Taiwan People's Party, the revision to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act passed by 60 votes to 39. Eligibility extends to any senior whose net consolidated income is either below the tax-filing threshold or subject to a marginal rate under 20 percent, currently equivalent to NT$1.38 million.

Proponents argue that the policy merely extends nationwide a benefit already offered in Taipei, where former mayor Ko Wen-je introduced it. Less affluent counties, however, have been unable to replicate the scheme, creating what supporters regard as an inequitable patchwork.

Health Minister Shih Chung-liang has voiced serious reservations, contending that the amendment erodes the principle that contributions should be proportionate to income. He warned that it could exacerbate intergenerational inequity, constrain the growth of the overall health budget and compel the government to divert revenue from other welfare priorities.

The controversy highlights a broader dilemma confronting a super-aged society: how to sustain universal healthcare when one-fifth of the population is elderly and accounts for over 42 percent of expenditure. The estimated annual cost is close to NT$39 billion.

opposition-controlled.ex: The opposition-controlled parliament blocked the plan.

others.ex: Some agreed, but others did not.

overall.ex: The overall cost was higher than planned.

party.en: a side in a deal or argument

passed.ex: Her grandfather passed away last year.

patchwork.en: a mix of different parts that do not match
patchwork.ex: The rules are a patchwork of local laws.

pays.ex: The company pays for staff training.

percent.ex: Ten percent of the class was absent.

pick.en: in "pick up the bill": to pay for something
pick.ex: The company will pick up the bill.

pioneered.en: was the first to do or use something
pioneered.ex: The town pioneered free bus travel.

policy.ex: The new housing policy starts in May.

population.en: all the people living in a place
population.ex: The population of Dublin is growing.

premium.ex: People pay a premium for organic food.

presidential.ex: The presidential election is in spring.

pressure.en: strong demand or force from people
pressure.ex: There is pressure on the company to cut prices.

principle.ex: Equal pay is a key principle.

priorities.ex: Health and schools are top priorities.

problems.ex: The main problem is the cost.

programmes.ex: The city runs many welfare programmes.

promise.en: to say you will surely do something
promise.ex: I promise to call you tomorrow.

proponents.ex: Proponents of the plan say it will save money.

proportionate.en: matching something in size or amount
proportionate.ex: The fine should be proportionate to the crime.

note.usage: 形容詞，常接 to：proportionate to income；反義 disproportionate；副詞 proportionately。

example.en: Fees should be proportionate to what families can pay.
example.zh: 收費應與家庭的負擔能力相稱。

noteHi.meaning: किसी चीज़ के अनुपात में, उचित मात्रा में।
noteHi.usage: अक्सर to के साथ: proportionate to income। विलोम disproportionate।
noteHi.exampleTr: शुल्क परिवारों की भुगतान क्षमता के अनुपात में होने चाहिए।

noteEs.usage: Suele ir con to: proportionate to income. Contrario: disproportionate.
noteEs.exampleTr: Las tarifas deberían ser proporcionales a lo que pueden pagar las familias.

noteJa.usage: to を伴うことが多い（proportionate to income）。反意語 disproportionate。
noteJa.exampleTr: 料金は家庭の支払い能力に見合うべきだ。

noteKo.usage: 흔히 to와 함께(proportionate to income). 반의어 disproportionate.
noteKo.exampleTr: 요금은 가정의 지불 능력에 비례해야 한다.

noteEn.meaning: matching something in size, amount or seriousness.

push.en: push back: move to a later time
push.ex: Bad weather may push the launch back a week.

pushed.ex: The storm pushed the opening back by a week.

qualify.en: to have the right to get

rate.ex: The population is growing at a slow rate.

reacted.en: did or said something because of an event

reflects.en: shows or is caused by something

regard.ex: Many regard him as the best player.

remarked.ex: She remarked that it was cold.

replicate.ex: Other towns tried to replicate the plan.

note.meaning: 複製、仿效（成功的做法、實驗結果）。
note.usage: 及物動詞，正式用語；常用於政策、研究：replicate a model / results。名詞 replication。

example.en: Poorer towns struggled to replicate the city's free bus scheme.
example.zh: 較窮的鄉鎮難以仿效該市的免費公車計畫。

noteHi.meaning: किसी सफल तरीके या परिणाम की नकल करना, दोहराना।
noteHi.usage: सकर्मक, औपचारिक; नीति और शोध में आम: replicate results।
noteHi.exampleTr: गरीब कस्बों को शहर की मुफ्त बस योजना दोहराने में कठिनाई हुई।

noteEs.usage: Verbo transitivo formal; habitual en políticas e investigación: replicate results.
noteEs.exampleTr: Los pueblos más pobres no lograron replicar el plan de autobuses gratis.

noteJa.meaning: （成功例や結果を）再現する、模倣する。
noteJa.usage: 他動詞・硬い表現。政策や研究で多い（replicate results）。名詞 replication。
noteJa.exampleTr: 貧しい町は市の無料バス制度を再現できなかった。

noteKo.usage: 격식 있는 타동사; 정책·연구에서 흔함(replicate results).
noteKo.exampleTr: 가난한 마을들은 시의 무료 버스 제도를 따라 하기 어려웠다.

noteEn.meaning: to copy something, such as a successful plan or result, so it happens again.

requiring.en: making something necessary by a rule
requiring.ex: A new rule is requiring masks on buses.

reservations.ex: I have reservations about the plan.

note.usage: 常用複數，接 about：have reservations about sth；without reservation = 毫無保留地。

example.en: Several doctors expressed reservations about the new policy.
example.zh: 幾位醫生對新政策表示疑慮。

noteHi.meaning: किसी चीज़ के बारे में शंकाएँ या आपत्तियाँ।
noteHi.usage: अक्सर बहुवचन, about के साथ: have reservations about।
noteHi.exampleTr: कई डॉक्टरों ने नई नीति पर आपत्ति जताई।

noteEs.usage: Suele ir en plural con about: have reservations about.
noteEs.exampleTr: Varios médicos expresaron reservas sobre la nueva política.

noteJa.usage: 通常複数形で about を伴う（have reservations about）。
noteJa.exampleTr: 数人の医師が新政策に懸念を示した。

noteKo.usage: 주로 복수형, about과 함께(have reservations about).
noteKo.exampleTr: 여러 의사가 새 정책에 우려를 표했다.

noteEn.meaning: doubts that make you not fully agree with something.

scheme.ex: The bike scheme is popular in Dublin.

senior.ex: A senior doctor checked the results.

serving.en: working in a role or duty

similar.ex: My bag is similar to yours.

small.ex: It's a small town in the west.

stretched.zh: stretched to breaking point：不堪負荷

subject.ex: All flights are subject to delays in winter.

suit.en: follow suit: do the same thing

super-aged.en: having more than 20% of people over 65

supporters.en: people who agree with and help an idea

sustain.ex: Farms cannot sustain life without water.

system.en: a set of rules or ways of working

taiwan.en: an island country in East Asia

tax.ex: You pay tax on your income.

taxable.en: you must pay tax on it

thinks.ex: He thinks the film is too long.

threshold.ex: Income above the threshold is taxed.

time.ex: For the first time, dentists will join.

tpp.en: the Taiwan People's Party, an opposition party

tpp's.en: belonging to the Taiwan People's Party

universal.ex: The plan did not win universal support.

voiced.en: said what you think or feel

young.ex: Young people often use social media.
